By the 1970s, hundreds of the tiny, enigmatic objects
had been found throughout the Middle East. Archaeologist
Denise Schmandt-Besserat was traveling to various
museums throughout four continents, cataloging the
objects, when she made a connection. Other, more recent
groups used small objects to record the numbers of animals
and amounts of grain exchanged in business transactions.
Such information led Schmandt-Besserat to determine
that the Uruk objects, which she began calling “tokens,”
had been used to count goods. Each token represented
one commodity, such as one lamb or one loaf of bread.
Using a one-to-one counting method, so that someone had
five jars of oil, he or she would also have five ovoid tokens
representing those jars. As the people of Uruk bought,
sold, and traded goods, some were exchanged for
with the proto-cuneiform on the Uruk tablets resembled
indentations of tokens. In addition to keeping track of
goods via tokens, the people of Uruk kept records on the
tablets. The first tablet recordings were made by pressing
tokens into the tablets while the clay was still wet.
Eventually, the people of Uruk began using a stylus to
